subject: Chemistry
question:
(a) What is the maximum electron population in each of the following?
(i) n=2 shell; (ii) 3d subshell; (iii) any sub-orbital.
(b) Give the set of quantum numbers for the first 2 electrons in the third shell.
modelAnswer:
(a) (i) The n=2 shell has s and p subshells (2s² 2p⁶), so the maximum is 8 electrons. (ii) The 3d subshell has 5 orbitals, so the maximum is 10 electrons. (iii) Any single sub-orbital (orbital) can hold a maximum of 2 electrons (Pauli exclusion principle).
(b) The third shell is n=3. The first two electrons go into the 3s orbital.
Electron 1: n=3, l=0, m_l=0, m_s=+1/2
Electron 2: n=3, l=0, m_l=0, m_s=-1/2

subject: Chemistry
question:
The osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving 1.0 g of haemoglobin in 100 cm³ of water is 4.13 kPa at 20 °C. Calculate
(a) concentration in the unit of g m⁻³; (b) the molar mass of the haemoglobin.
modelAnswer:
(a) Mass = 1.0 g; volume = 100 cm³ = 100 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Concentration = 1.0 g/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 1.0 × 10⁴ g m⁻³ (10 000 g m⁻³).

(b) π = cRT, where c is in mol m⁻³.
π = 4.13 kPa = 4130 Pa; T = 20 + 273 = 293 K; R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
c = π/RT = 4130/(8.314 × 293) = 4130/2436 = 1.695 mol m⁻³.
Molar mass = mass concentration/molar concentration = 10 000/1.695 = 5.90 × 10³ g mol⁻¹ (about 5900 g mol⁻¹).
(Note: real haemoglobin has a molar mass of about 64 500 g mol⁻¹. The figures in the paper give 5900 g mol⁻¹, which is the expected answer.)

subject: Chemistry
question:
In the complex ion, [CrBrCl(NH3)4]+,
(a) Give the oxidation number of Cr in the complex
(b) What is the coordination number of Cr in the complex?
(c) Draw the structure of the complex ion and indicate the co-ordinate covalent bonds involved.
(d) What is the shape of the ion?
modelAnswer:
(a) Let the oxidation number of Cr be x. Br⁻ = −1, Cl⁻ = −1, NH₃ = 0.
x + (−1) + (−1) + 4(0) = +1 → x = +3.

(b) Coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded to Cr = 1 (Br) + 1 (Cl) + 4 (N of NH₃) = 6.

(c) Structure: Cr³⁺ at the centre of an octahedron, with the six ligands at the six corners: four NH₃, one Br⁻ and one Cl⁻. All six Cr–ligand bonds are coordinate (dative) covalent bonds: each ligand donates a lone pair into an empty orbital of Cr³⁺. The lone pair comes from the N atom in each NH₃, and from the halide ion for Br⁻ and Cl⁻. Draw each bond as an arrow from the ligand to Cr (L → Cr), and put the whole ion in square brackets with a + charge.
(The Br and Cl may be next to each other (cis, 90°) or opposite each other (trans, 180°), so the ion has two geometrical isomers; either drawing is acceptable.)

(d) Octahedral.

subject: Chemistry
question:
(a) What are isotopes?
(b) Five atoms have the following composition:
Atom M: 8p, 8e, 8n
Atom N: 8p, 7e, 8n
Atom P: 8p, 8e, 7n
Atom Q: 7p, 8e, 8n
Atom R: 8p, 8e, 9n
Which of these are isotopes?
modelAnswer:
(a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers).

(b) Isotopes must have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons:
• M: 8p, 8n (oxygen-16)
• P: 8p, 7n (oxygen-15)
• R: 8p, 9n (oxygen-17)
M, P and R are isotopes (of oxygen).

• N: 8p, 8n but only 7 electrons. It has the same nucleus as M, so it is not an isotope of M; it is a positive ion (O⁺) of oxygen-16. (Its nucleus is still an isotope of P and R.)
• Q: 7p, 8n, 8e. It is a different element (nitrogen), present as the ion N⁻, so it is not an isotope of the others.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Consider the following elements or most stable ions of the elements in the periodic table: Mg, Hg, P, Cl, Na and Ar.
(a) Which of these elements is most electropositive?
(b) Which of these elements is a metal with the lowest melting point?
(c) Which of these elements has lowest electron affinity?
(d) Which of these elements has highest ionisation potential?
(e) Which of these elements has highest electronegativity?
modelAnswer:
(a) Na (Sodium) is an alkali metal in Group 1, making it the most electropositive among the choices.
(b) Hg (Mercury) is a liquid at room temperature and has a very low melting point (-38.8 °C).
(c) Ar (Argon) is a noble gas with a stable octet, so it has the lowest (virtually zero) electron affinity.
(d) Ar (Argon) has the highest ionization potential because it is a noble gas with a stable, full outer shell, making it very hard to remove an electron.
(e) Cl (Chlorine) is a highly reactive halogen in Group 17, making it the most electronegative element listed.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Calculate the mass of the following:
(a) 6.023 × 10²³ atoms of nitrogen.
(b) 6.023 × 10²³ molecules of nitrogen.
(c) 1 mole of carbon(II) oxide.
(d) 0.4 mole of nitrogen(IV) oxide.
(e) 2 moles of boron atoms.
modelAnswer:
Relative atomic masses: N = 14, C = 12, O = 16, B = 10.8 (about 11).
6.023 × 10²³ particles = 1 mole (Avogadro's number).

(a) 6.023 × 10²³ atoms of N = 1 mol of N atoms. Mass = 1 × 14 = 14 g.
(b) 6.023 × 10²³ molecules of N₂ = 1 mol of N₂. Mass = 1 × 28 = 28 g.
(c) 1 mol of CO: mass = 12 + 16 = 28 g.
(d) 0.4 mol of NO₂: M = 14 + 2(16) = 46 g mol⁻¹. Mass = 0.4 × 46 = 18.4 g.
(e) 2 mol of B atoms: mass = 2 × 10.8 = 21.6 g (22 g if B = 11 is used).
(Boron's relative atomic mass is 10.8, not 10.)

subject: Chemistry
modelAnswer:
(a) 1 mole of aqueous KBr has higher entropy. Dissolving a solid in water increases disorder (aqueous ions have more freedom of movement than a rigid lattice).
(b) 1 mole of SO3 has higher entropy. SO3 is a larger, more complex molecule with more vibrational modes than SO2.
(c) Sea water in mid-summer at 23 °C has higher entropy. Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy and random motion of particles.
(d) 3 moles of oxygen gas has higher entropy. Entropy is an extensive property; 3 moles of any gas have more entropy than 2 moles of a similar gas (Ozone, O3).
(e) 1 mole of CO2 gas has higher entropy. Gases have significantly higher entropy than solids due to the free movement of particles.

subject: Chemistry
question: A 0.372 mole dm⁻³ KMnO4 solution was titrated against a solution of hydrogen peroxide which had been diluted 10 times. A 25 cm³ of the diluted peroxide solution was neutralised by 26.20 cm³ of KMnO4 solution. Calculate the molarity of the original peroxide solution.
modelAnswer:
Note: the paper says the peroxide was "neutralised". This is a redox titration, not a neutralisation.

Equation (acid solution): 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O.
Mole ratio MnO₄⁻ : H₂O₂ = 2 : 5.

Moles of KMnO₄ = 0.372 × 26.20/1000 = 9.746 × 10⁻³ mol.
Moles of H₂O₂ in 25 cm³ of diluted solution = 9.746 × 10⁻³ × 5/2 = 2.437 × 10⁻² mol.
Concentration of diluted H₂O₂ = 2.437 × 10⁻²/(25/1000) = 0.975 mol dm⁻³.
The original solution was 10 times more concentrated:
Original molarity = 0.975 × 10 = 9.75 mol dm⁻³.

subject: Chemistry
question:
(a) State two factors responsible for the softness of group 1 elements of the periodic table.
(b) Why is the enthalpy of hydration of calcium higher than that of potassium ion?
modelAnswer:
(a) 1. Large atomic radii, meaning the valence electron is far from the nucleus and held loosely. 2. Low effective nuclear charge and strong shielding, resulting in weak metallic bonding (only one valence electron per atom is delocalized).
(b) Ca²⁺ has a higher charge density (higher charge of +2 vs +1 for K⁺, and a smaller ionic radius) than K⁺. The stronger electrostatic attraction between Ca²⁺ and the polar water molecules releases more energy upon hydration.

subject: Chemistry
question:
State the number of phases in each of the following:
(a) air; (b) a mixture containing oil and water; (c) a mixture of salt and sand; (d) a mixture of ethanol and water; (e) addition of CaCO3 to a mixture containing CaO and CO2 gas.
modelAnswer:
A phase is a part of a system that is uniform throughout and separated from other parts by a boundary.
(a) Air: 1 phase. All gases mix completely to form one uniform phase.
(b) Oil and water: 2 phases (two immiscible liquid layers).
(c) Salt and sand: 2 phases (two different solids, each a separate phase).
(d) Ethanol and water: 1 phase (they are miscible and form one solution).
(e) CaCO₃ added to CaO and CO₂: 3 phases. CaCO₃(s) and CaO(s) are two different solids, so each is a separate phase, and CO₂(g) is a third phase. (This is the classic phase-rule example CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g).)

subject: Chemistry
question:
In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution of copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI), explain what would happen at the electrodes if:
(i) platinum electrodes are used. Write where necessary, ionic equations to support your answer.
(ii) copper electrodes are used. Write where necessary, ionic equations to support your answer.
modelAnswer:
(i) With inert platinum electrodes:
Cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺ ions are discharged in preference to H⁺. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (copper is deposited).
Anode (oxidation): OH⁻ ions are discharged in preference to SO4²⁻. 4OH⁻(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g) + 4e⁻ (oxygen gas is evolved).
The blue color of the solution fades.
(ii) With active copper electrodes:
Cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (copper is deposited).
Anode (oxidation): The copper anode dissolves. Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
The blue color of the solution remains constant, and copper is effectively transferred from anode to cathode (used in electrorefining).

subject: Chemistry
question: Comment on the observation that iron sheet rusts less rapidly when coated with zinc (galvanised) than when coated with tin (tinned).
modelAnswer:
Zinc is more electropositive (higher in the electrochemical series) than iron. If the zinc coating is scratched, zinc acts as the sacrificial anode and corrodes preferentially, protecting the iron (cathode).
Tin is less electropositive than iron. If the tin coating is scratched, iron becomes the anode and corrodes faster because it is in contact with a less reactive metal (tin), setting up a local galvanic cell. Thus, galvanizing offers better protection.

subject: Chemistry
question: Calculate the change in potential of a copper electrode at 300 K, if the concentration of copper(II) tetraoxosulphate solution in contact with it was changed from 0.5 to 0.001 mol dm⁻³.
modelAnswer:
For Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s), the Nernst equation is
E = E° + (2.303RT/nF) log[Cu²⁺], with n = 2.
At 300 K: 2.303RT/nF = (2.303 × 8.314 × 300)/(2 × 96 500) = 5744/193 000 = 0.0298 V.

Change in potential: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = 0.0298 × log([Cu²⁺]₂/[Cu²⁺]₁)
= 0.0298 × log(0.001/0.5)
= 0.0298 × log(0.002)
= 0.0298 × (−2.699)
= −0.080 V.

The electrode potential decreases by about 0.080 V (it becomes less positive), because there are fewer Cu²⁺ ions to be reduced.

subject: Chemistry
question:
An element, A has an atomic number of 29.
(i) Write full electron configuration of A;
(ii) Is the element, A in s-, p- or d-block of the periodic table?
(iii) State any five characteristic properties of A.
(iv) What is the principal oxidation number of A?
(v) Show whether the oxide of A is likely to be acidic, basic or amphoteric substance.
(vi) State the expected bond type of the oxide in a(v) above.
modelAnswer:
(i) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
(ii) d-block (it is copper, a transition metal).
(iii) 1. Forms colored compounds (e.g., blue Cu²⁺). 2. Exhibits variable oxidation states (+1, +2). 3. Forms complex ions (e.g., [Cu(NH3)4]²⁺). 4. Acts as a catalyst. 5. Has high density and melting point.
(iv) The principal oxidation state is +2 (Cu²⁺ is more stable in aqueous solution than Cu⁺).
(v) The oxide (CuO) is a basic oxide. It reacts with acids to form salts. (It is not amphoteric).
(vi) The bond type is ionic (with some covalent character).

subject: Chemistry
question:
(i) What is allotropy?
(ii) Name the two allotropes of carbon.
(iii) Which of them conducts electricity and which would not.
(iv) Give a suitable explanation to support your choice.
(c) Give two other elements that exhibit allotropy in the periodic table.
modelAnswer:
(i) Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different physical forms in the same state, having different structural arrangements.
(ii) Diamond and Graphite (also fullerenes).
(iii) Graphite conducts electricity; diamond does not.
(iv) In graphite, each carbon atom is sp² hybridized and bonded to three others, leaving one delocalized electron per atom. These delocalized electrons are free to move along the layers, allowing it to conduct. In diamond, all four valence electrons of each carbon are used in strong sigma bonds in a rigid tetrahedral lattice, leaving no free electrons.
(c) Sulfur (rhombic and monoclinic) and Phosphorus (white and red).

subject: Chemistry
question: What is a phase? Give one characteristic of a phase. Sketch the phase diagram of each of the following: (i) water; (ii) carbon(IV) oxide.
modelAnswer:
A phase is a physically distinct, homogeneous part of a system, separated from other parts by a definite boundary.
Characteristic: a phase has the same composition and physical properties throughout. (Other acceptable: it can be separated mechanically from other phases.)

(i) Water phase diagram: pressure (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis), with three regions: solid (ice, left), liquid (middle/top) and vapour (bottom/right). Three lines meet at the triple point (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm = 611 Pa):
• the solid–liquid (melting) line slopes slightly backwards (to the left), a negative slope;
• the liquid–vapour (boiling) line rises to the critical point (374 °C, 218 atm);
• the solid–vapour (sublimation) line runs below the triple point.
At 1 atm, water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

(ii) CO₂ phase diagram: the same three regions and lines, but the solid–liquid line slopes forwards (positive slope). The triple point is at −56.6 °C and 5.11 atm, and the critical point at 31.1 °C and 73 atm. At 1 atm (below the triple-point pressure) solid CO₂ sublimes at −78 °C without melting.

subject: Chemistry
question:
(i) Outline any three essential features of diagram c(i).
(ii) Explain any two differences between the diagrams, c(i) and c(ii) above.
modelAnswer:
Note: the paper refers to "diagram c(i)" and "c(ii)". These are the diagrams sketched in 13(a)(i) and (ii).

(i) Three essential features of the water diagram (any three):
1. The solid–liquid line has a negative slope, because ice is less dense than water, so increasing pressure lowers the melting point.
2. There is a triple point (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm), where solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium.
3. There is a critical point (374 °C, 218 atm), above which liquid and vapour cannot be distinguished.
4. Each region (area) represents one phase; along each line two phases are in equilibrium.

(ii) Differences (any two):
1. Slope of the solid–liquid line: negative for water, positive for CO₂ (solid CO₂ is denser than liquid CO₂).
2. Triple-point pressure: water's (0.006 atm) is far below 1 atm, so at normal pressure ice melts to liquid water. CO₂'s (5.11 atm) is above 1 atm, so at normal pressure solid CO₂ (dry ice) sublimes directly to gas, and liquid CO₂ exists only under pressure.
3. Positions of the triple and critical points: water's triple point is at 0.01 °C, CO₂'s at −56.6 °C; water's critical temperature is 374 °C, CO₂'s only 31.1 °C.

subject: Chemistry
question:
(i) State Raoult's law for ideal solutions.
(ii) A mixture of 0.2 mole of methanol A and 0.5 mole of propanol B has a total vapour pressure of 40 mmHg at 298K. If the mixture obeys Raoult's law, calculate the vapour pressure of pure B at 298K, given that the pressure of pure A is 20 mmHg at 298K.
modelAnswer:
(i) Raoult's Law states that the partial vapour pressure of each component in an ideal solution is equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction in the mixture.
(ii) Moles of A = 0.2, Moles of B = 0.5. Total moles = 0.7.
Mole fraction of A (Xa) = 0.2/0.7 = 0.2857. Mole fraction of B (Xb) = 0.5/0.7 = 0.7143.
P_total = Pa + Pb = Xa*P°a + Xb*P°b.
40 = (0.2857 × 20) + (0.7143 × P°b).
40 = 5.714 + 0.7143 P°b.
34.286 = 0.7143 P°b.
P°b = 34.286 / 0.7143 = 48.0 mmHg.

subject: Chemistry
question: State Moseley law of periodic table.
modelAnswer: Moseley's Law states that the square root of the frequency of the X-rays emitted by an element is directly proportional to its atomic number (Z). Mathematically, √f = a(Z - b). This established that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental property determining an element's position in the periodic table.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Define the following periodic properties using an appropriate chemical equation in each case:
(i) ionisation energy; (ii) electron affinity.
modelAnswer:
(i) Ionization energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
Equation: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻
(ii) Electron affinity is the energy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions.
Equation: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g)

subject: Chemistry
question:
State and account for the trend in the properties listed in (b) above:
(i) across a period; (ii) down a group in the periodic table.
modelAnswer:
(i) Across a period (left to right):
• Ionisation energy generally increases. Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so shielding hardly changes and the outer electrons are held more tightly; the atomic radius decreases. (Small dips occur, e.g. from Be to B and from N to O.)
• Electron affinity generally becomes more negative (more energy released), for the same reason: the nucleus attracts an added electron more strongly. Noble gases (and Group 2 elements) are exceptions, with almost zero or positive values.

(ii) Down a group:
• Ionisation energy decreases. A new shell is added each time, so the atomic radius and shielding increase, and the outer electron is further from the nucleus and easier to remove.
• Electron affinity generally becomes less negative, because an added electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. (Exception: F has a less negative electron affinity than Cl, because F is so small that the added electron is repelled by the crowded electrons.)

subject: Chemistry
question: Arrange the ions, F⁻, Na⁺, N³⁻ and Mg²⁺ in the order of increasing size. Advance reason for your answer.
modelAnswer:
Order: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < N³⁻.
Reason: All these ions are isoelectronic (they all have 10 electrons, the same electron configuration as Neon). For isoelectronic species, the ionic radius decreases as the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases. Mg has 12 protons, Na has 11, F has 9, and N has 7. The higher the nuclear charge, the stronger the attraction on the 10 electrons, resulting in a smaller radius.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Account for the following observations:
(i) Tin and lead form tetravalent ions but carbon and silicon do not.
(ii) NaCl is insoluble in organic solvent whereas AlCl3 is substantially soluble in organic solvent.
(iii) The melting points of group 14 elements decrease down the group of the periodic table.
(iv) PCl5 is more stable than PCl3 on the other hand, BiCl3 is unstable but BiCl5 is stable.
(v) Excessive inhalation of carbon(II) oxide is toxic to humans.
modelAnswer:
Note on (iv): the statement about bismuth is printed the wrong way round. In reality BiCl₃ is the stable chloride and BiCl₅ does not exist (it is unstable). The answer explains the real trend.

(i) Forming a 4+ ion requires removing four electrons, and the sum of the first four ionisation energies is very large. C and Si are small atoms with very high ionisation energies, so they cannot form M⁴⁺ ions; instead they share electrons and form covalent compounds (e.g. CH₄, SiCl₄). Sn and Pb are much larger atoms with lower ionisation energies (they are metals), so they can form ions in the +4 state, as in SnO₂ and PbO₂, which have considerable ionic character. (Lead more commonly forms Pb²⁺ because of the inert-pair effect.)

(ii) NaCl is an ionic compound: its lattice is held by strong electrostatic forces, and non-polar organic solvents cannot solvate the ions or supply the energy to break the lattice, so it is insoluble ('like dissolves like'). AlCl₃ is largely covalent: the small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion polarises Cl⁻ strongly (Fajans' rules). It exists as covalent Al₂Cl₆ molecules, which dissolve in organic solvents.

(iii) The bonding changes down the group. C (diamond) and Si have giant covalent structures with very strong bonds (very high melting points). Ge is also giant covalent but with weaker, longer bonds. Sn and Pb are metals with weaker metallic bonding. As atoms get larger, bonds get longer and weaker, so less energy is needed to melt the solid: C (about 3550 °C) > Si (1410 °C) > Ge (937 °C) > Sn (232 °C). Pb (327 °C) is slightly higher than Sn, a minor exception to the trend.

(iv) The +5 state becomes less stable down Group 15 because of the inert-pair effect: the ns² electrons of heavy elements like Bi are held tightly (poorly shielded by the filled d and f subshells) and are reluctant to take part in bonding. P readily uses all five valence electrons (expanding its octet using 3d orbitals) to form PCl₅, although PCl₅ dissociates to PCl₃ + Cl₂ on heating. Bi keeps its 6s² pair inert and forms BiCl₃, which is stable; BiCl₅ does not form.

(v) Carbon(II) oxide (CO) combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells about 200–250 times more strongly than oxygen does, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin. This haemoglobin can no longer carry oxygen, so tissues are starved of oxygen, causing headache, dizziness, unconsciousness and death by asphyxia. CO is also colourless and odourless, so it is not noticed.

subject: Chemistry
question:
(i) What is hydrogen bonding?
(ii) List two conditions that must be satisfied before hydrogen bond can be formed.
modelAnswer:
(i) Hydrogen bonding is a strong electrostatic attraction between a highly electronegative atom (like N, O, or F) and a hydrogen atom that is covalently bonded to another highly electronegative atom.
(ii) Conditions: 1. A hydrogen atom must be attached directly to a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N). 2. The electronegative atom must have at least one lone pair of electrons available for interaction.

subject: Chemistry
question: List any four laws of chemical combination of atoms.
modelAnswer:
1. Law of Conservation of Mass (Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction).
2. Law of Definite Proportions (A compound always contains the same elements in exactly the same proportions by mass).
3. Law of Multiple Proportions (When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio).
4. Law of Reciprocal Proportions (The ratio of the masses of two elements that combine with a fixed mass of a third element is the same as the ratio in which they combine with each other).

subject: Chemistry
question:
(i) Zinc oxide was prepared in the laboratory by using two experimental procedures. In the first method, 0.325g of zinc combined with 0.08g of oxygen to form the metal oxide. In the second procedure, 1.625g of zinc reacted with 0.4g of oxygen to produce the oxide of the metal. Calculate the percentage by mass of the metal in the oxide in each of the methods.
(ii) Which of the laws of chemical combination do the above data illustrate? Justify with suitable reason.
(iii) Cite any limitation of the law.
modelAnswer:
(i) Method 1: Total mass = 0.325 + 0.08 = 0.405 g. % Zn = (0.325 / 0.405) × 100 = 80.25%.
Method 2: Total mass = 1.625 + 0.4 = 2.025 g. % Zn = (1.625 / 2.025) × 100 = 80.25%.
(ii) The Law of Definite Proportions (or Constant Composition). The percentage composition of the metal (Zn) in the oxide is the same (80.25%) regardless of the method of preparation or the mass of reactants used.
(iii) Limitation: It does not hold true for compounds that have variable isotopic compositions, or non-stoichiometric compounds (berthollides).

subject: Chemistry
question:
In the Haber process for an industrial manufacture of ammonia, 15 cm³ of nitrogen was mixed with 80cm³ of hydrogen gas under suitable condition.
(i) Determine the reaction stoichiometry.
(ii) Determine which of the reactant gases is in excess and by what amount.
(iii) Determine the volume of reaction product.
(iv) Calculate the volume of residual gas mixture at the end of the reaction.
modelAnswer:
(i) N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). Stoichiometric ratio is 1 vol N2 : 3 vol H2 : 2 vol NH3.
(ii) 15 cm³ N2 requires 15 × 3 = 45 cm³ H2. Since we have 80 cm³ H2, H2 is in excess. Excess H2 = 80 - 45 = 35 cm³.
(iii) 15 cm³ N2 produces 15 × 2 = 30 cm³ NH3.
(iv) Residual gases: Unreacted H2 = 35 cm³. NH3 produced = 30 cm³. Total volume = 35 + 30 = 65 cm³. (N2 is completely consumed as it is the limiting reactant).
